lines.text: Recap — the chapter in short
RECAP
People across India eat widely different food, and the difference is not
random. It follows the crops that grow in each region, which follow soil and
climate, and is then shaped by culture, religion and taste.
Culinary practices have changed sharply within living memory — from
chulha to gas stove, from sil-batta to mixer-grinder —
driven by new
technology, better transport and faster communication. The changes
brought real gains and some real losses.
• Food is a mixture of components. The five major nutrients are
carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals. Food also supplies
roughage and water, which are essential but are not nutrients.
• Carbohydrates and fats supply energy and are called energy-giving foods.
Fat carries more energy per gram than carbohydrate and is the body's store.
• Proteins build and repair the body and are called body-building foods.
Growing children and athletes need proportionally more.
• Vitamins and minerals are needed in tiny amounts and are called protective
nutrients. Going short of one for long enough causes a specific deficiency
disorder — scurvy, rickets, beriberi, goitre, anaemia — each with its own
symptoms and its own food remedy.
• Roughage supplies no nutrients and cannot be digested; that is why it
works, giving the digestive system bulk to move waste along. Water carries
nutrients in, carries waste out, and holds body temperature steady.
• Starch, fat and protein can be detected with simple tests: iodine turns
starch blue-black, fat leaves a translucent oily patch on paper, and copper
sulfate with caustic soda turns protein violet. Most foods contain more than
one nutrient.
A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in
the right amounts, with enough roughage and water. What is balanced
depends on age, sex, activity, health and way of life.
• Junk foods carry plenty of energy from sugar and fat and little else. Millets
are called nutri-cereals because they carry fibre and minerals along with their
carbohydrate, and they grow on less water.
• Food miles are the distance food travels from producer to consumer.
Shorter is cheaper, fresher, less polluting, and better for nearby farmers.
Wasted food wastes everything that went into producing it.
